218  THE SAVOY MALE AND FEMALE COLLEGE

    Sixth, and last, Mr. Halsell was a philanthropist in an unusual way. He was the poor boys' and poor girls' friend. I never knew of him to turn any boy or girl away who was otherwise unable to pay for it, being turned away who came to Mr. Halsell. He probably often went with money out of his own pocket. It is true that he had a hard time working teachers their salaries, but he always took care of the boys and girls who wanted an education.

STUDENTS AND EX-STUDENTS

    We have in our audience today a most unusual group of persons, being a large number of the present student body, and a considerable audience comprising the surrounding citizens. I speak with greater freedom before ex-students of the latter group, and therefore can speak advisedly in saying that it is very desirable for the ex-students and the students to visualize the sacrifices, hardships, privations and personal discomforts through which those students of the old days went in those days to get their education, and in their efforts to secure an education.

    To much credit should be given to Mr. Halsell and his associates for their sacrificial leadership in those days when an education was not so easily obtained as it is today. I want you of the present generation to think well upon the fine character and achievement of the present-day student body of the Savoy School, and I to those who may hear me who are of the school age to think well. You might not enjoy the conveniences which are provided here. We make no sacrifice and went to no hardship like the students of other days, and yet, if you were forced to go through what they went through to get an education, most of you present would get along with your education then. I think we lacked conveniences and that we lacked comforts and that we lacked opportunities to get a good education. In our day we were greatly in advance of the day of our forefathers, and so it is in the day that we live in.

    To him who is so fortunate as to have nearly completed education in an institution but who has had to depend upon one's efforts to get a good education, the education has been more enduring. To those who are either untrained person in life, I should like to encourage you to take advantage of every opportunity which you have in trying to secure a complete education, to encourage you, if I may, to continue your own education until it is completed. How does it benefit a man or woman who is not mentally fully equipped to compete with others who are fully trained and who experienced such and such as the case, wait until he is not too late that you have thrown away the greatest asset now available to you.
notes: Continuation of Gus W. Thomasson's dedication address.
